propositions.text: George Yankson is a Ghanaian citizen who claimed refugee protection in Canada based on his sexual orientation as a gay man.
propositions.quote: George Yankson is a citizen of Ghana who claimed refugee protection in Canada on the basis of his sexual orientation as a gay man.

propositions.text: The Refugee Protection Division dismissed his claim because it did not believe he is gay.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dismissed his claim because it did not believe that he is gay.

propositions.text: The Refugee Appeal Division dismissed his appeal.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismissed his appeal.

propositions.text: He now seeks judicial review of the RAD decision.
propositions.quote: He now seeks judicial review of the RAD decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Yankson, a Ghanaian, claimed refugee protection as a gay man; RPD and RAD dismissed his claim and appeal; he seeks judicial review.

propositions.text: Applicant states he has always been attracted to men but did not act due to illegality in Ghana.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that he has always been attracted to men, but did not act on his feelings because homosexuality is forbidden and illegal in Ghana.

propositions.text: He had his first sexual experience in November 2013 at age 18; partner died in car accident shortly after.
propositions.quote: He states that he had his first sexual experience in November 2013, when he was 18 years old. His partner was killed in a car accident shortly after their relationship started.

propositions.text: He began another relationship soon after; in March 2014, he and partner were discovered at school and he was forced to flee and leave school.
propositions.quote: He began a relationship with another partner a short time later, and that relationship continued for some time. In March 2014, the Applicant and his partner were discovered at school, and the Applicant was forced to flee to escape. His mother was informed of what had happened, and he was forced to leave the school.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says he was attracted to men but acted cautiously due to illegality; had two relationships; forced to flee school after discovery.

propositions.text: Applicant endured harassment and mistreatment due to sexual orientation in his community.
propositions.quote: The Applicant says he endured harassment and mistreatment by people in his community because of his sexual orientation.

propositions.text: He visited grandmother in another city; she discovered him with partner and ordered him to leave.
propositions.quote: He eventually left to visit his grandmother in another city, but during his stay there, she discovered him with this partner, and ordered him to leave.

propositions.text: He returned to live with mother; mother’s bakery lost customers and closed due to hostility over his sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: He returned to live with his mother. The Applicant says that his mother’s bakery business lost customers and eventually closed because people were hostile towards her because of his sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says he faced community harassment, was expelled by grandmother, returned to mother whose bakery closed due to hostility over his orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant was attacked by neighbour who burned his arm with hot iron.
propositions.quote: The Applicant says he was attacked by a neighbour who burned his arm with a hot iron.

propositions.text: He decided to flee Ghana; obtained student visa in March 2016 with agent’s help; arrived in Canada May 2016 and claimed refugee protection.
propositions.quote: He then decided that he had to flee Ghana. With the assistance of an agent, he obtained a student visa in March 2016 and arrived in Canada in early May 2016. He claimed refugee protection upon his arrival.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was attacked, decided to flee Ghana, obtained student visa, arrived in Canada in May 2016, and claimed refugee protection.

propositions.text: RPD dismissed claim due to lack of credibility and little weight to supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD dismissed the Applicant’s claim, finding that his testimony lacked credibility and that the supporting evidence he filed should be given very little weight.

propositions.text: RPD noted significant discrepancies in testimony about first relationship duration and contradictions with Basis of Claim Form.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that there were significant discrepancies in the Applicant’s testimony about how long his first relationship had lasted, and that his evidence contradicted the information in his Basis of Claim Form.

propositions.text: Applicant’s inability to state full name, birth date, or address of second partner during second port of entry interview undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: It also found that his inability to state the full name, date of birth or address of his second partner when he was questioned during his second port of entry interviewalso undermined his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: RPD dismissed claim for lack of credibility due to discrepancies and inability to identify second partner details at interview.

propositions.text: Applicant provided letters from mother, cousin, friend, and info on LGBT community attendance in Canada.
propositions.quote: The supporting evidence provided by the Applicant included letters from his mother and cousin in Ghana, together with a letter from a friend in Canada as well as information that he attended community group meetings involving the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community in Canada.

propositions.text: RPD discounted this evidence because it was unsworn, authors unavailable to testify, and LGBT attendance did not establish sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: This evidence was discounted by the RPD, because it was not contained in sworn documents, the authors were not available to testify, and the information about his participation in the LGBT community in Canada did not establish his sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: RPD discounted unsworn letters and LGBT community attendance evidence as insufficient to establish sexual orientation.

propositions.text: RPD concluded Applicant had not established he is gay and dismissed refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The RPD therefore concluded that the Applicant had not established that he is gay, and it dismissed his refugee claim.

propositions.text: Applicant appealed to RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicant appealed this to the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: RPD dismissed claim for failure to establish sexual orientation; Applicant appealed to RAD.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed appeal, agreeing RPD did not err in concluding Applicant was never in same-sex relationship in Ghana.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismissed the appeal, finding that the RPD had not erred in concluding that the Applicant was never in a same sex relationship in Ghana.

propositions.text: Applicant’s inability to give second partner’s last name or birth date at port of entry impugned credibility, as did contradictions about relationship end date.
propositions.quote: It found that the Applicant’s inability to give his second partner’s last name or date of birth to the officer at the port of entry did impugn his credibility, as did the contradictions about when that relationship had ended.

propositions.text: RAD referred to SOGIE Guideline noting discomfort with authority and fear could affect reluctance to disclose sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The RAD referred to the Chairperson’s Guideline 9: Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression (the SOGIE Guideline) and noted that discomfort with authority figures and fear of being turned away could conceivably affect a claimant’s reluctance to disclose his or her sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: RAD dismissed appeal, agreed RPD’s credibility findings, and referenced SOGIE Guideline on claimant reluctance to disclose orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant explained fear of return to Ghana due to debts and lack of funds to repay them.
propositions.quote: On the facts of this case, however, the RAD concluded that the Applicant had explained in some detail his fear of being sent back to Ghana because he owed money to people and he did not have the funds to repay them.

propositions.text: Applicant only mentioned sexual orientation at end of second interview.
propositions.quote: It was only at the end of his second interview that the Applicant made any reference to his sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant expressed concern about inability to visit family in Ghana after refugee claim process explained.
propositions.quote: In addition, when the process of making a refugee claim was explained to him, the Applicant expressed concern that he would not be able to go back to Ghana to visit his family.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Applicant feared return due to debts, mentioned sexual orientation late, and worried about visiting family after claim process explained.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant’s belated sexual orientation statement could be discomfort but more credible explanation was truthfulness about fear of debts.
propositions.quote: While I acknowledge that his belated statement about his sexual orientation could be due to discomfort with the officers, the more simple explanation is more credible to me: the [Applicant] was telling the truth when he was first asked about his fear.

propositions.text: Applicant’s desire to return to Ghana to repay lenders supports credibility of fear explanation over anti-gay violence fear.
propositions.quote: This explanation is also consistent with his desire to return to Ghana to visit his family after he had earned some money to repay his lenders, which money would not protect him if his real fear was of anti-gay violence.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Applicant’s late sexual orientation disclosure likely truth about fear of debts, supported by desire to return to repay lenders.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant’s evidence about first same-sex relationship vague and contradictory, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found that the Applicant’s evidence regarding his first same sex relationship was vague and contradictory, and combined with the other difficulties with his evidence, this undermined his credibility.

propositions.text: RAD rejected procedural fairness argument about RPD giving little weight to supporting documentation without notice or response opportunity.
propositions.quote: The RAD rejected the argument that the RPD had breached procedural fairness by giving little weight to the supporting documentation the Applicant had filed, without giving him notice or an opportunity to respond.

propositions.text: RPD’s weighing of evidence and preference for sworn testimony over unsworn letters is ordinary and lawful process.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the RPD engaged in the ordinary process of weighing evidence, and that it was simply giving effect to the well-known legal principle that sworn documentation and live testimony by witnesses will be given more weight than unsworn letters.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed supporting evidence should be given little weight in establishing sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s review of this evidence confirmed that it should be given little weight in establishing the Applicant’s sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Applicant’s relationship evidence vague, rejected procedural fairness claim, and upheld RPD’s evidence weighting approach.

propositions.text: RAD concluded Applicant had not established he is gay or perceived to be gay and rejected claim.
propositions.quote: Based on its review of the evidence, the RAD concluded that the Applicant had not established that he is gay or perceived to be gay, and therefore it rejected his claim.

paragraphs.summary: RAD concluded Applicant failed to establish he is or is perceived as gay and rejected his claim.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD erred by failing to follow SOGIE Guidelines properly.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of this decision, arguing that the RAD erred by: (i) failing to properly follow the SOGIE Guidelines;

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD denied procedural fairness by requiring sworn affidavits and live witnesses.
propositions.quote: (ii) denying the Applicant procedural fairness by requiring sworn affidavits and live witnesses;

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD misapprehended evidence on crucial points.
propositions.quote: (iii) misapprehending the evidence on crucial points.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD erred by not following SOGIE Guidelines, denying procedural fairness, and misapprehending evidence.

propositions.text: Standard of review for first and third issues is reasonableness per Huruglica 2016 FCA 93 para 35.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for the first and third issues is reasonableness: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93 at para 35.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness is assessed similarly to correctness but court must determine if process was fair and reasonable per Khosa 2009 SCC 12 para 43 and CPR 2018 FCA 69 para 54.
propositions.quote: The issue of procedural fairness is assessed in a manner which resembles the correctness standard, but in the end a reviewing court must determine whether the process was fair and reasonable in the circumstances: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43; Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54.

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review is reasonableness for first and third issues; procedural fairness assessed for fairness and reasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review concerns substantive outcome and reasoning process requiring justification, transparency, intelligibility per Igloo Vikski 2016 SCC 38 para 18.
propositions.quote: The key question in a judicial review on the standard of reasonableness is summarized in Canada (Attorney General) v Igloo Vikski Inc, 2016 SCC 38, [2016] 2 SCR 80: [18] Reasonableness review is concerned with the reasonableness of the substantive outcome of the decision, and with the process of articulating that outcome.

propositions.text: Reasoning must show justification, transparency, intelligibility per Dunsmuir 2008 SCC 9 para 47.
propositions.quote: The reasoning must exhibit “justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process”: Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190, at para. 47.

propositions.text: Outcome and reasons must show result within range of possible outcomes per Newfoundland Nurses 2011 SCC 62 para 14.
propositions.quote: The substantive outcome and the reasons, considered together, must serve the purpose of showing whether the result falls within a range of possible outcomes: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 708, at para. 14.

propositions.text: Adequacy of reasons is not alone basis for review but reasons should adequately explain decision basis per Newfoundland Nurses para 18 and Canada Post 2010 FCA 56 para 163.
propositions.quote: While the adequacy of a tribunal’s reasons is not on its own a discrete basis for judicial review, the reasons should “adequately explain the bases of [the] decision”: Newfoundland Nurses, at para. 18, quoting from Canada Post Corp. v. Public Service Alliance of Canada, 2010 FCA 56, [2011] 2 F.C.R. 221, at para. 163 (per Evans J.A., dissenting), rev’d 2011 SCC 57, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 572.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness review requires justified, transparent, intelligible reasoning showing outcome within possible range; reasons should adequately explain decision.

propositions.text: Judicial review on reasonableness focuses on whether decision-maker engaged with evidence applying correct legal test.
propositions.quote: a key concern is whether the process and decision indicate that the decision-maker truly “engaged” with the evidence, applying the appropriate legal test.

propositions.text: Standard is not perfection; deference is due especially for factual inquiries within expertise and policy context.
propositions.quote: The standard is not perfection. It must be recalled that Parliament assigned the task of conducting the initial inquiry into the facts to the administrative decision-maker. Deference is due to a decision-maker, especially in a context where the inquiry is primarily factual, the subject-matter is within the decision-maker’s area of expertise, and where greater exposure to the nuances of evidence or a greater awareness of the policy context may provide an advantage.

paragraphs.summary: Court states reasonableness review asks if decision-maker engaged with evidence and legal test; deference is due; standard not perfection.

propositions.text: If decision-maker’s reasoning chain is understandable and shows engagement, decision is generally reasonable per Komolafe 2013 FC 431.
propositions.quote: If the chain of reasoning of the decision-maker can be understood, and if it shows that this type of engagement occurred, the decision will generally be found to be reasonable: see Komolafe v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 431.

propositions.text: Decision-maker need not mention every piece of evidence or step in analysis; omission is not reviewable error.
propositions.quote: It is not a reviewable error for the decision-maker to omit reference to every piece of evidence that was considered, or to fail to mention a particular step in the sequence of analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Reasonable decisions show engagement with evidence; omission of some evidence or steps is not reviewable error.

propositions.text: Reviewing court cannot ignore or replace reasons actually provided; additional reasons must supplement not supplant per Delta Air Lines 2018 SCC 2 para 24.
propositions.quote: A decision cannot be upheld because of what it might or ought to have said, if doing so involves ignoring or discounting the reasoning that was actually expressed in the decision. As Chief Justice McLaughlin (as she then was) said in Delta Air Lines Inc. v Lukács, 2018 SCC 2, [2018] 1 SCR 6 at para 24: “In other words, while a reviewing court may supplement the reasons given in support of an administrative decision, it cannot ignore or replace the reasons actually provided. Additional reasons must supplement and not supplant the analysis of the administrative body.”

paragraphs.summary: Court cannot ignore or replace reasons given; additional reasons must supplement, not supplant, administrative analysis.

propositions.text: RAD decision is unreasonable due to focus on microscopic, tangential, or inaccurate evidence statements.
propositions.quote: I find the decision of the RAD to be unreasonable because of the accumulation of instances in which its reasons focus on microscopic, tangentially relevant or inaccurate statements of the evidence.

propositions.text: There may be reasonable bases to discount testimony and documentation, but RAD’s reasons do not rely on these for credibility findings.
propositions.quote: While I find that there may have been reasonable bases to discount the Applicant’s testimony and supporting documentation, the actual reasons expressed by the RAD do not rely on these as a basis for its credibility findings.

propositions.text: Decision is unreasonable and must be sent back for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: The decision is unreasonable and must be sent back for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD decision unreasonable due to flawed reasoning and orders reconsideration.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD failed to follow SOGIE Guidelines fully in evidence consideration.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the RAD failed to follow the letter and spirit of the SOGIE Guidelines in its consideration of all of the evidence.

propositions.text: RAD mentioned Guidelines and followed them for port of entry credibility but not for other evidence, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: It mentions the Guidelines and appears to follow them in its assessment of the credibility of the Applicant’s statements at the port of entry, but not in relation to any of the other evidence. This is not reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD failed to fully follow SOGIE Guidelines; court finds partial adherence unreasonable.

propositions.text: Guidelines are not binding but must be applied or explained if not followed.
propositions.quote: The Guidelines are not binding, but they must be applied by decision-makers or an explanation must be given for not following them.

propositions.text: RAD cites Guidelines and shows application regarding contradictions in Applicant's port of entry evidence.
propositions.quote: In this case the RAD cites the Guidelines and then demonstrates how it is applying them in the context of its consideration of the ontradictions and difficulties with the Applicant’s evidence at the port of entry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Guidelines must be applied or explained if not followed and finds RAD applied them to contradictions in Applicant's port of entry evidence.

propositions.text: Agrees Applicant that RAD's consideration of Guidelines on other evidence is unclear.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that it is not evident whether or how the RAD considered the Guidelines in its assessment of any of the other evidence.

propositions.text: Unclear consideration alone is insufficient to overturn the decision.
propositions.quote: On its own, however, this is not a sufficient basis to overturn the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees Applicant that RAD's consideration of Guidelines on other evidence is unclear but finds this alone insufficient to overturn the decision.

propositions.text: RAD engaged in microscopic analysis of details to discount credibility or probative value.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to a number of instances in which the RAD engaged in a microscopic analysis of a particular detail as its basis to discount the credibility or probative value of the information.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues RAD used microscopic analysis of details to discount credibility or probative value.

propositions.text: Applicant gave contradictory evidence about schools attended; visa application school differs from port of entry and RPD hearing statements.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the Applicant gave contradictory evidence about the schools he attended, noting that in the student visa application and Basis of Claim form he submitted, the Applicant stated he attended one school while at the port of entry he gave the name of another school.

propositions.text: Applicant admitted visa application was fraudulent at port of entry but reverted to that school at RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: At the RPD hearing, he reverted to the school in his student visa application, though he had admitted at the POE that the visa application was fraudulent.

propositions.text: RAD rejected Applicant's explanation of stress and fatigue for wrong info at port of entry.
propositions.quote: The RAD rejected the Applicant’s explanation that he was tired and stressed when he gave the wrong information at the port of entry.

propositions.text: RAD found Applicant truthful at port of entry and fabricated narrative about sexual orientation linked to boarding school attendance.
propositions.quote: Again, a simple explanation is more credible to me: the [Applicant] was telling the truth when he was first asked about his education at the POE. In my view, the evidence is consistent with a fabricated narrative about the [Applicant’s] sexual orientation.

propositions.text: RAD concluded Applicant reverted to fraudulent visa school names to support boarding school narrative in Basis of Claim.
propositions.quote: Since the BOC narrative depended on the [Applicant] attending boarding school, he reverted to the school names in the fraudulent visa application, contradicting his spontaneous first declaration at the POE.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Applicant gave contradictory school evidence, rejected stress explanation, and concluded Applicant fabricated sexual orientation narrative linked to boarding school attendance.

propositions.text: Applicant argues refugee narrative does not depend on boarding school attendance; RAD's finding is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that this reasoning is flawed because his refugee narrative is not dependent in any way on his attendance at a boarding school.

propositions.text: Applicant's sexual encounters were not at boarding school residences, contradicting RAD's basis for credibility finding.
propositions.quote: His first sexual encounter was at his partner’s house, and while he and his second partner were discovered having sex near their school, it was not in a residence or any facility associated with a boarding school.

propositions.text: RAD's finding that narrative depended on boarding school attendance is unclear and irrational.
propositions.quote: It is not clear why the RAD found that the narrative “depended on” his attendance at a boarding school in the face of this evidence, and this is not a reasonable or rational basis to find his evidence to be lacking in credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues his refugee narrative does not depend on boarding school attendance and RAD's contrary finding is unreasonable and unclear.

propositions.text: RAD gave little weight to letter from Applicant's friend, citing lack of partner's testimony and inability to test basis of belief.
propositions.quote: The RAD gave little weight to a letter from the Applicant’s friend in Canada, since it found that the letter “indicates that person’s belief but it does not purport to be from a partner who would have a more reliable view of the [Applicant’s] sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Applicant submits RAD contradicts SOGIE Guidelines by requiring oral testimony over written evidence and not engaging with letter content.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that this finding is in direct contradiction to the SOGIE Guidelines, because the RAD does not demonstrate an understanding that it may be difficult or impossible for a person to obtain evidence from sexual partners, and it is, in effect, requiring oral testimony rather than weighing written evidence in support of a claim.

propositions.text: No indication RAD engaged with letter content; findings based on form rather than substance.
propositions.quote: There is no indication the RAD actually engaged with the content of the letter, but rather made its findings on matters of form.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD gave little weight to a friend's letter; Applicant argues this contradicts SOGIE Guidelines and RAD ignored letter content.

propositions.text: RAD rejected cousin's letter as not credible due to incorrect number of Applicant's sisters, implying fabrication.
propositions.quote: I find that this letter is not credible and further impugns the credibility of the [Applicant] because it names and repeatedly refers to his two younger sisters, contradicting the [Applicant’s] BOC, which names three younger sisters from his parents’ marriage, all under the age of 15.

propositions.text: RAD found a true family member would know number of sisters; letter fabricated to support false claim.
propositions.quote: I find that a true family member would know how many sisters the Applicant has, and that this letter was fabricated to support a false claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD rejected the cousin's letter as not credible due to incorrect sister count, concluding it was fabricated.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD's focus on sister number is microscopic and irrelevant to refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that this is a microscopic analysis of an irrelevant point.

propositions.text: BOC form shows third sister has different last name; RAD's rejection lacks analysis of letter's content or context.
propositions.quote: The basis of claim form that the RAD refers to indicates that his third sister has a different last name. It is not reasonable for the RAD to completely reject the letter on this basis, without any analysis of its actual contents, the context within which it was written or any other features that may affect its probative value.

propositions.text: RAD seizes on irrelevant point to discount credibility and attribute fraudulent intent.
propositions.quote: This is another example of the RAD seizing on an irrelevant point to discount the Applicant’s credibility and to attribute fraudulent intent to him.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD's rejection of cousin's letter based on sister number is irrelevant, lacks content analysis, and unfairly attributes fraud.

propositions.text: RAD gave no weight to letters from uncle and uncle's wife due to uncle's involvement in BOC form and credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RAD gave no weight to the letters provided by the Applicant’s uncle or the uncle’s wife, because it found that the uncle had assisted the Applicant to complete the original Basis of Claim form, and had signed the form indicating that he had interpreted it for the Applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant contradicted uncle's role; RAD found uncle's letter not credible due to alleged false statement and urging Applicant to sign untrue statement.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contradicted this in his testimony, and so the RAD found at paragraph 23 that the uncle’s letter should be given no weight since “the allegation that this person himself signed an untrue statement about the interpretation of the BOC and urged the [Applicant] to sign an untrue statement calls into question his credibility.”

paragraphs.summary: RAD gave no weight to uncle's letters due to uncle's role in BOC form and credibility concerns from alleged false statements.

propositions.text: Applicant notes errors in BOC form show uncle tried to help but made mistakes; RAD's conclusion of fraud is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points to a number of incorrect or inaccurate statements in the original basis of claim form, and suggests that this makes it evident that although the uncle did his best to help the Applicant complete the form, it is obvious that he made a number of mistakes.

propositions.text: Unreasonable for RAD to seize on one error to conclude fraudulent intent by uncle and Applicant.
propositions.quote: It is unreasonable for the RAD to seize on one such error and to then conclude that it demonstrates fraudulent intent on the part of the uncle and the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues errors in BOC form reflect uncle's mistakes, making RAD's fraud conclusion unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant points out RAD failed to refer to letter from Applicant's mother with personal knowledge of key events.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points out that the RAD failed to refer to the letter from the Applicant’s mother, despite her personal knowledge of the key events that led him to flee Ghana and claim refugee status.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant notes RAD failed to consider letter from his mother with key event knowledge.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RAD breached procedural fairness by not addressing submission about RPD ignoring key evidence in unsworn letters and not advising Applicant of concerns.
propositions.quote: Finally, the Applicant argues that the RAD breached procedural fairness when it failed to meaningfully address its submission that the RPD failed to consider the key evidence in the letters because they were not sworn and without advising the Applicant of its concerns.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RAD breached procedural fairness by not addressing submission on RPD ignoring unsworn letters and not advising Applicant.

propositions.text: Respondent contends RAD reasonably found RPD did not err applying general evidence rules preferring sworn and oral evidence.
propositions.quote: The Respondent contends that the RAD reasonably found that the RPD did not err in applying the general rules of evidence, preferring sworn evidence to unsworn letters, and oral testimony to written documentation.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent contends RAD reasonably found RPD did not err preferring sworn and oral evidence over unsworn letters.

propositions.text: Respondent submits RAD's credibility assessment deserves deference and is supported by record contradictions and omissions.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the decision and outcome must be viewed as an organic whole, and that the RAD’s assessment of credibility is owed significant deference.

propositions.text: Record supports RAD's finding Applicant not credible due to contradictions and omissions at point of entry and about partners.
propositions.quote: In this case, there was ample support in the record for the RAD’s finding that the Applicant was not credible, including the contradictions and basic omissions from his narrative at the point of entry. The Applicant gave contradictory evidence about the length of his first relationship, and failed to provide basic information about his second partner. In addition, the Applicant contradicted himself about when the most recent relationship ended.

propositions.text: RAD did not err in finding omissions and contradictions affected Applicant's credibility, citing Ogaulu case.
propositions.quote: The RAD did not err in finding that these omissions and contradictions about the core of the claim affected the Applicant’s credibility: Ogaulu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 547 at para 20.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD's credibility assessment is supported by record contradictions and omissions and deserves deference.

propositions.text: Respondent argues discrepancies about school attended were material and relevant to credibility.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Respondent argues that the discrepancies in the Applicant’s evidence about which school he attended were material.

propositions.text: Applicant claimed attending same school as second partner, caught having sex there, and expelled; school evidence relevant.
propositions.quote: He claimed that he attended the same school as his second partner, that they were caught in a sexual encounter at that school and that he was then expelled.

propositions.text: RAD did not err in finding contradictions about school attendance undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: This makes the evidence about which school he attended relevant, and the RAD did not err in finding that the contradictions undermined the Applicant’s credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues discrepancies about school attended were material and RAD did not err in finding contradictions undermined credibility.

propositions.text: Respondent argues RAD reasonably considered documentary evidence credibility in light of Applicant's credibility findings and totality of evidence.
propositions.quote: It was both reasonable and appropriate for the RAD to consider the credibility and reliability of the documentary evidence in light of its earlier findings about the Applicant’s credibility, and the decision makes clear that the RAD carefully considered the evidence in its totality.

propositions.text: Details Applicant points to show RAD's careful examination; court should not re-weigh evidence.
propositions.quote: The details that the Applicant points to are in fact indications of the care with which the RAD examinedthat evidence. It is not the role of the Court to re-weigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RAD reasonably considered documentary evidence and court should not re-weigh evidence.

propositions.text: Court agrees RAD's decision is not reasonable due to microscopic analysis without evidence weighing.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that the RAD’s decision is not reasonable, because several significant evidentiary findings were based on a microscopic analysis of particular, specific aspects of the evidence, and there is no indication that the RAD engaged in any analysis or weighing of the evidence on its merits.

propositions.text: Supreme Court says court should not ignore or replace RAD's own explanation of findings.
propositions.quote: To recall the words of the Supreme Court, it is not the role of the Court to ignore or replace the words the RAD actually used to explain its findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees RAD's decision is unreasonable due to microscopic analysis without weighing evidence, citing Supreme Court guidance.

propositions.text: RAD discounted cousin's letter solely due to sister number discrepancy without engaging with letter substance.
propositions.quote: The RAD discounted the supportive letter from the cousin because he referred to the Applicant’s two sisters and contradicted the evidence showing that the Applicant has three sisters.

propositions.text: Applicant notes third sister has different last name, possibly explaining omission; RAD's basis unclear.
propositions.quote: As the Applicant notes, the number of sisters the Applicant has is irrelevant to his refugee claim, and his third sister has a different last name, which may explain why the cousin did not mention here.

propositions.text: RAD did not explain why sister number discrepancy justified discounting letter or engage with letter's substance.
propositions.quote: It is not otherwise evident why this is a basis to discount the cousin’s letter. The RAD mentions that the cousin’s letter outlines his suspicions about the Applicant’s sexual orientation and recounts what he was told by the Applicant’s mother, but these are not referred to as the basis for the RAD’s conclusion.

propositions.text: RAD's credibility finding based only on sister number is not engagement with evidence substance or probative weight.
propositions.quote: Instead, the RAD explains its credibility finding only with reference to the number of sisters. This is not an indication that the RAD actually engaged with the substance of the evidence before assessing its credibility or probative weight.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD discounted cousin's letter solely on sister number discrepancy without engaging with letter's substance or explaining basis.

propositions.text: RAD analyzed uncle's letter by focusing on one BOC form contradiction without assessing letter substance or context.
propositions.quote: The RAD analyzed the letter from the uncle in a similar manner. The RAD seizes on a prior basis of claim form that the Applicant completed with the assistance of the uncle, notes that he contradicted the statement on that form that it had been translated to him, and then concludes that this called into question the uncle’s credibility to such an extent that the letter was given no weight.

propositions.text: RAD did not explain how other BOC form mistakes were analyzed, showing microscopic analysis without explanation.
propositions.quote: Again, this is not an analysis of the substance of the letter, or the context within which it was written, and it involves a microscopic analysis of one aspect of the evidence, without any explanation for how the other evident mistakes in the original basis of claim form were analyzed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD focused on one BOC form contradiction to discredit uncle's letter without analyzing substance or context.

propositions.text: Court agrees there are omissions and contradictions raising credibility questions.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent’s argument that there are significant omissions and contradictions in the Applicant’s evidence, which could raise legitimate questions about his credibility.

propositions.text: RAD must consider all evidence on merits and analyze it reasonably despite credibility issues.
propositions.quote: However, this does not remove the RAD’s obligation to consider the rest of the evidence on its merits, and to demonstrate that it analyzed and considered the evidence in a reasonable manner.

propositions.text: RAD's decision falls short on key fronts in analyzing and considering evidence reasonably.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s decision falls short on several key fronts in this regard, as demonstrated above.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees credibility issues exist but finds RAD failed to reasonably analyze and consider all evidence on its merits.

propositions.text: Judicial review of a RAD decision is a deferential reasonableness review, not a line-by-line error search.
propositions.quote: Judicial review of a RAD decision should not be a line-by-line treasure hunt for error, but rather the court is required to examine the reasons and outcome to determine whether they demonstrate that the result falls within the range of reasonable outcomes.

propositions.text: Parliament assigned evidence review to RPD and RAD; court must not usurp that role.
propositions.quote: Parliament has assigned the task of reviewing and assessing the evidence to the RPD and then the RAD. It is not the role of this Court to usurp that role.

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness, not perfection.
propositions.quote: The standard is not perfection, but rather reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that judicial review of RAD decisions is deferential, focusing on reasonableness, not error hunting or usurping the RAD's role.

propositions.text: The evidentiary record contained much that could support the RAD's conclusion on the claim's merits.
propositions.quote: there was much in the evidentiary record that could have supported the RAD’s conclusion on the merits of the claim.

propositions.text: However, the RAD's explanation at key points in its analysis cannot be ignored.
propositions.quote: I find that at several key points in its analysis the RAD’s explanation for its reasoning simply cannot be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the record could support RAD's conclusion but the RAD's reasoning at key points is problematic.

propositions.text: It is unclear if the RAD applied the SOGIE Guidelines to all evidence.
propositions.quote: It is not clear whether the RAD applied the SOGIE Guidelines to its consideration of all of the evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD's explanation for questioning credibility focused on minor details, not substance or context.
propositions.quote: its explanation for questioning the credibility of the Applicant, his cousin and his uncle are explained with reference to microscopic analysis of tangential details rather than the substance or overall context for the evidence.

propositions.text: The letter from the Applicant’s mother, providing direct evidence, was not mentioned by the RAD.
propositions.quote: The letter from the Applicant’s mother, which provides more direct evidence, is not mentioned.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD unclear on applying SOGIE Guidelines, focusing on minor details and ignoring key evidence like the mother's letter.

propositions.text: The RAD based key determinations on irrelevant or minor details without analyzing evidence substance or context.
propositions.quote: it appears that it has based key determinations on largely irrelevant or minor points of detail, without any analysis of the substance of the evidence or the context within which it was given.

propositions.text: The court can follow the RAD's reasoning chain but finds it flawed at key points.
propositions.quote: I find that while I can follow the chain of reasoning of the RAD, at several key points it appears that...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD's reasoning flawed by reliance on minor details without substantive evidence analysis, though the reasoning chain is traceable.

propositions.text: Reasoning must show justification, transparency and intelligibility as required by Dunsmuir and Jakutavicius.
propositions.quote: The reasoning does not demonstrate “justification, transparency and intelligibility” within the decision-making process, as required by Dunsmuir (and see the discussion in Jakutavicius v Canada (Attorney General), 2011 FC 311 at para 31).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RAD's reasoning lacks required justification, transparency, and intelligibility per Dunsmuir and Jakutavicius.

propositions.text: The RAD decision is unreasonable for reasons explained above.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out above, I find the decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Because of this, the procedural fairness argument need not be addressed in detail.
propositions.quote: In light of my conclusion on this issue, it is not necessary to address the procedural fairness argument in any detail.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD decision is unreasonable and declines to address procedural fairness further.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is granted, the RAD decision is overturned, and the matter is sent back to a different RAD panel.
propositions.quote: I am therefore granting the application for judicial review. The RAD decision is overturned and the matter is sent back for reconsideration by a different panel of the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, overturns the RAD decision, and remands the matter to a different RAD panel.

propositions.text: No question of general importance was proposed or arises for certification.
propositions.quote: No question of general importance was proposed for certification, and none arises in this case.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed, the RAD decision is overturned, and the matter is remanded to a different RAD panel.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division is overturned. The matter is sent back for reconsideration by a different panel of the Refugee Appeal Division.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms no general importance question arises and reiterates the judicial review allowance, RAD decision overturn, and remand.
